title: I'm Terrified: Struggling to Take My Own Advice on This Graduation Day
author: Daniel Golazeski
summary: A retiring teacher reflects on the tension between his own long-standing advice — that teachers should attend graduation — and the fear that his voice injury will prevent him from fully showing up for his students one last time. Golazeski spent his career quietly standing by the exit to offer final smiles and farewells, believing graduation was a sacred opportunity for teachers to demonstrate genuine gratitude. Now, forced to retire due to a vocal condition, he grapples with the prospect of not being able to speak a word to the students who approach him, potentially reducing him to writing notes on paper. He reflects on how the fear of revealing his injury — and the selfish wish to preserve his students' memories of him with a strong voice — is real but ultimately irrelevant, because between risking vulnerability and risking his students thinking he forgot them, there is no real choice. The essay is a quiet meditation on presence, vocation, and what it means to show up for students even when it costs something personal.
points: Graduation is one of the last opportunities a teacher has to demonstrate that students mattered — attending is an act of gratitude and closure for both parties, not an intrusion on students' day.

The fear of revealing physical vulnerability (a voice injury) in front of students is real but secondary to the vocational obligation to show up; Golazeski recognizes this as 'both paralyzing and irrelevant.'
The asymmetry of regret is decisive: you may feel worse immediately after going but will feel better for the rest of your life — whereas not going guarantees lasting regret.
Teachers project their own discomfort onto students when they skip graduation, imagining they are protecting students' day rather than acknowledging their own avoidance.
Retirement from teaching due to disability does not end the relationship with students; the bonds formed in the classroom extend past the formal role and obligate continued presence.
quotes: Graduation is a chance to give one last smile. One last, 'Good luck!' One last, 'Thank you!' One last demonstration that we're glad and grateful we had the chance to be their teacher. One last time to show them we're happy they were a part of our lives for a few brief years. Seems like an evening well spent to me.
There's even a selfish part of me that would prefer my students' last impression of 'Mr. G' to be a memory of the me who had a strong voice.

Strangely, those fears are both paralyzing and irrelevant. I don't believe in fate, but it does feel like my actions are already decided. If my choices are (a) risk revealing how injured my voice actually is, or (b) risk my students thinking I forgot about them, then there is no choice.

I honestly don't know how I will feel as I drive home from my former school's graduation. It's very possible that, in that moment, I will feel worse for attending the ceremony. However, I am absolutely certain that the next day, a year from now, and for the rest of the time I have on this earth, I will feel better for having gone.

Seeing my students celebrate their accomplishments gave me some of the best memories from my career. That's why I always advised my student teachers to go to their school's graduation, even if — especially if — they're not required to.
